title: Rate of Change: What It Really Means

scenes.title: What does rate of change actually mean?
body: Suppose a table goes from (1, 4) to (3, 10).
We are measuring how much y changes for each 1-unit change in x.
scenes.narration: Suppose a table gives you the points one, four and three, ten. Here is the idea: rate of change tells you how much the output changes for each one-unit change in the input. It is not just the change in y. It compares the change in y to the change in x.

scenes.title: This is where students often mix it up
body: y changes by 6, but x changes by 2.
So the rate is not 6. We must compare both changes.
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. From four to ten, y increases by six, so six looks tempting. But x did not increase by one; it increased by two. A rate is a comparison. We divide the six-unit change in y by the two-unit change in x, giving three.

scenes.title: Why dividing works
body: 6 units of y-change happen over 2 units of x-change.
6 ÷ 2 tells us the change for exactly 1 unit of x.
scenes.substitution: 1 step in x → 3 steps in y
scenes.narration: Notice why the division works. Six units of vertical change happen across two units of horizontal change. Dividing six by two converts that total change into a per-one-unit rate. So every increase of one in x corresponds to an increase of three in y.

scenes.title: Connect it to slope
body: For a linear relationship, rate of change is the slope.
A constant rate of 3 means the line rises 3 for every 1 to the right.
scenes.narration: For a linear relationship, this rate of change is exactly the slope. A slope of three means right one, up three. That is why the same number appears in a table, a graph, and an equation: all three are describing the same constant relationship.

scenes.title: Quick check
body: A rate of 3 predicts y should rise by 6: 4 + 6 = 10.
scenes.narration: Quick check: starting at one, four, increase x by two. If the rate is three per one unit of x, then y should increase by six. Four plus six is ten, matching the second point. So the key idea is this: rate of change is change in y per one unit of change in x, not just the change in y. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
